reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A consequence of gastric or bariatric surgery, or vagotomy, in which food empties too rapidly into the small intestine
Early dumping occurs within about half an hour of eating and combines gastrointestinal symptoms (bloating, cramps, diarrhoea) with vasomotor features (flushing, palpitations, light-headedness)
Late dumping occurs one to three hours after eating and is due to reactive hypoglycaemia with tremor, sweating, and confusion
Symptoms are typically provoked by meals rich in rapidly absorbed carbohydrate
Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, supported where needed by a provocation test or documentation of postprandial hypoglycaemia
First-line management is dietary modification with smaller, more frequent low-carbohydrate meals and separating solids from liquids
Refractory cases may need pharmacological therapy to slow transit or, rarely, surgical revision
reference.pathophysiology: Dumping syndrome follows loss of normal gastric reservoir and pyloric control after surgery, allowing hyperosmolar gastric contents to pass rapidly into the small bowel. In early dumping, the osmotic load draws fluid into the lumen, causing distension and diarrhoea, and triggers release of vasoactive gut hormones that produce the vasomotor symptoms. In late dumping, rapid delivery and absorption of carbohydrate provokes an exaggerated insulin (and incretin) surge that outlasts the glucose load, resulting in reactive hypoglycaemia one to three hours after the meal.
additionalDifferentials: Carcinoid or other neuroendocrine flushing syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Structured clinical scoring of postprandial symptoms
Oral glucose provocation test with monitoring of glucose, haematocrit, and pulse
Documentation of postprandial hypoglycaemia during symptoms
Gastric emptying study to confirm rapid emptying
Upper endoscopy or contrast study to assess the postsurgical anatomy
redFlags: Severe or recurrent hypoglycaemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms
Symptoms suggesting a mechanical complication such as afferent loop obstruction
Features suggesting an endocrine tumour rather than dumping
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with dietary modification, and symptoms often lessen over time; a minority have persistent, disabling symptoms requiring pharmacological or surgical measures.
pitfalls: Overlooking late dumping as a cause of postprandial hypoglycaemic spells after gastric surgery
Failing to give thorough dietary advice before escalating to drugs or surgery
Confusing dumping with afferent loop syndrome or gastroparesis
Attributing vasomotor symptoms to anxiety rather than to rapid emptying
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Begin with dietary modification as first-line therapy: small, frequent low-carbohydrate meals, avoidance of rapidly absorbed sugars and separation of solids from liquids
Advise lying down after meals to reduce early vasomotor symptoms and add soluble fibre or viscosity-increasing agents to slow gastric emptying
Treat late dumping (reactive hypoglycaemia) with carbohydrate restriction and consider acarbose to slow intestinal carbohydrate absorption
Add a somatostatin analogue such as octreotide for vasomotor and gastrointestinal symptoms refractory to diet
Monitor nutritional status and glucose, and correct deficiencies arising from altered post-surgical intake
Refer for surgical revision or continuous enteral feeding in the minority with persistent, disabling symptoms
Involve a dietitian and the surgical team for coordinated management after gastric or bariatric surgery
